name: Yuri Kochiyama
tagline: The woman who held Malcolm X as he died — and spent sixty years fighting for everyone else
story:
On February 21, 1965, gunshots tore through the Audubon Ballroom in Harlem. As the crowd scattered in terror, a small Japanese-American woman rushed toward the stage instead of away from it. Yuri Kochiyama cradled Malcolm X's head in her lap as he lay dying — a moment captured in one of the most iconic photographs of the civil rights era. She was 44 years old, a mother of six, and the last gentle presence Malcolm would ever know.

But Yuri's path to that ballroom had been forged in injustice decades earlier. After Pearl Harbor, her family was torn from their home in San Pedro, California, and imprisoned at the Jerome internment camp in Arkansas. Her father, arrested by the FBI on the day of the attack, was denied medical care and died shortly after release. The trauma didn't break her — it radicalized her. She emerged from the camps with a quiet fury and an unshakable conviction that no community should face oppression alone.

In Harlem, where she moved with her husband Bill, Yuri became a bridge between movements that others saw as separate. She linked the Japanese-American redress movement with Black liberation, Puerto Rican independence with Native American sovereignty. Her small apartment became a legendary hub of activism — part salon, part war room, part post office for political prisoners. She wrote thousands of letters to incarcerated activists, visited them faithfully, and made sure the world didn't forget them.

Yuri Kochiyama kept fighting until she was 93 years old, passing away on the same day as Malcolm X's birthday in 2014 — a coincidence so poetic it felt like a final act of solidarity. She proved that grit isn't always loud. Sometimes it's a woman who keeps showing up, keeps writing letters, keeps building bridges between struggles, for sixty relentless years.
